Yeah, this is basically my life.

Programming

I started coding when I was seven and it’s still my favourite hobby almost a decade later. Here are the projects I’m proudest of, and where it all started.

My GitHubGot something technical?

How I got into it

I started with Lua

My first language was Lua. I quickly moved on to Python, which is still my favourite and the one I know best. I also use JavaScript, HTML and CSS, and I’ve done some stuff with C++. I do a lot of web development, like this website and Namesake.

I consider myself lucky to have started programming before the age of AI. I think it’s unlikely I would ever have bothered to learn properly if I were starting now. I think that’s something we will notice...

Since then I’ve made physics simulations, 2D and 3D games, websites, mobile apps and Windows software. One of my first big projects was a YouTube channel where I made Roblox Studio and Lua tutorials.

I also made a website for Friends of St John’s Garden, a local park group. It’s on Volunteering.

Why I like programming

  • If something you want doesn't exist, make it and now it does!
  • I’ll be honest, it doesn’t involve interacting with people so I can just spend hours in my headspace. I like that it’s solitary when I want it to be, and collaborative when it matters. Namesake taught me the second half.
  • There’s always another problem to solve - something that is pointed out a lot by my family, after spending all day on a project.

Things I’ve made and contributed to

The projects I’m proudest of

A before-and-after screenshot of the homepage support map, and a screenshot of the live directory.

Open source · age 16

Namesake

What it is

Namesake is a US non-profit that publishes free name-change guides and tools for trans people, built by and for the trans community. Its code is open source, so anyone can propose changes.

What I did

Five changes accepted into Namesake’s code in my first week, the summer after Year 11. A pull request is a proposed change that the maintainers review and accept. Mine:

  • fixed the interactive support map on the homepage, where clicking a state had stopped working
  • fixed a bug that stopped images loading for developers
  • rewrote how website addresses are shown in the support directory, with tests
  • added seven organisations to the directory
  • made the developer tooling set itself up

I also proposed the blank-forms download and wrote the issue for it; the maintainer built it. I’m now doing some research for the project, which is still in progress.

What was hard

The map fix took the longest: I spent a lot of time running scripts in the browser to debug why the bug was happening. It was a real ‘problem solving’ bug fix instead of a typo. Hovering over a state moved its shape to the top of the map so its outline showed, and that reordering was what broke clicking. The fix was to draw the outlines on a separate layer so hovering doesn’t move anything, which the maintainer and I finished together after review.

The cause matters to me, with everything going on in the US. But let’s not get political now…

What I took from it

My first project involving true collaboration between many people in a large codebase. I learnt many best practices for collaborating with code. It also got me further invested in the cause.

My merged changesVisit Namesake
  • 24 July 2026: #717 support map click fix, co-authored with the maintainer after code review
  • 27 July 2026: #725 local image fix, #728 address formatting with tests, #729 seven directory entries (co-authored), #735 tooling setup
  • 11 September 2026: the blank-packet download, #753, built by the maintainer from my issue #722
  • Role: volunteer contributor, age 16

Web development · since age 14

This website

What it is

The site you’re on: hand-written HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no build step.

What I did

Everything, including the part most people never see: end-to-end, visual regression and accessibility tests across three browsers, Lighthouse performance budgets, linting, checks that run on every change, a public status page with uptime monitoring, and analytics.

As I incorporate AI more into my work, it being such a powerful tool, I have been offloading the more tedious jobs, like design. My favourite code is always the backend so getting AI to write some CSS is a big relief. All of the initial website was hand-coded, before AI was big.

What was hard

Learning all the best practices and techniques. I use this website as a way to experiment, so adding a new feature usually means learning how to do it properly first: a public status page, visual regression tests, accessibility checks, performance budgets, and analytics that only load after consent.

What I took from it

I have been able to implement many cool features, many of which cannot be seen. I have learnt much about coding techniques and third-party-app integration. It is also a test of whether I can keep a project up-to-date consistently through a long period of time.

How this site worksThe codeStatus page
  • Online since 2025; still changing most weeks
  • Hosted on GitHub Pages; every change is checked by GitHub Actions; Better Stack checks the live pages every three minutes
  • Automated tests added in August 2026

Two or three screenshots of the guides and the backup app.

Built for my grandparents · age 13

TechAssist

What it is

Simple written and video guides for everyday computer tasks, plus a separate one-click encrypted backup app, made for my grandparents.

What I did

It was my biggest project at the time: about how many lines of Python, using Tkinter, which other modules. I spent a massive amount of time on this project.

What was hard

Designing for people who aren’t confident with computers: every step had to make sense without me there to explain it. Keeping it all consistent as the codebase grew was hard too.

It was an early build for family rather than a finished app: restoring a backup was manual, and the guide videos were hosted on Dropbox and aren’t online any more.

What I took from it

One sentence. Also: what your grandparents said.

  • Built at 13, over about three months; written in Python with Tkinter
  • Guide videos were hosted on Dropbox and are no longer online

Using AI

How I actually use it

I think I was very lucky to learn to code before AI could do it all for me.

How you use AI now, in two or three sentences: what you hand to it, what you don’t, and how you check its work.

With a research team

Weekly calls at LSHTM

I have weekly calls with a TB vaccine modelling team at LSHTM about bringing AI into how they build their model.

More on Volunteering

Where I started

My earliest projects

Some are useful, most are not. :) None of these are polished. All of them taught me something.

  • Age 10 Chrome Dino: my first game, a Python version of the Chrome dinosaur game. Code
  • Age 12 Minesweeper: made in Python, with three difficulty levels. Just like the original, really. Code
  • Age 14 Bouncing Ball Physics Simulation: balls bounce off one another with gravity and friction. You can tell the graphics weren't very good, but I put my focus on flexibility and realistic physics. Code
  • Age 14 Game of Life: click or drag to add live cells, then see which patterns survive. Playable: clone the repo and run it. Code
  • Age 14 SplitMate: my first mobile app, to work out how a group should split shared expenses. Code
  • Ages 10 to 13 leopardbookshop on YouTube: I taught Roblox Studio and Lua; just over 400 subscribers and 108,000 views. The channel is still up. The channel

Volunteering, the online kind

Got something technical you need help with?

If there’s something technical you want doing, get in touch and we can talk about it. I’m happy to volunteer for charities, community groups and other small organisations. Mostly that means websites and web apps, like this site and Namesake, but also Python tools and small desktop apps.

Anything big, small, long or short term: a whole website, a fix, a tool, or a second pair of eyes on something broken. Just tell me roughly what you need.
